title: Earth's Building Blocks Came From Its Own Neighborhood, Study Finds
summary:
For decades, planetary scientists have debated where Earth's raw material came from. Many thought 6 to 40 percent of it drifted in from the outer Solar System, beyond Jupiter. That idea helped explain how Earth got water and other volatile substances — materials that turn to gas easily.

New research challenges that picture. Paolo Sossi and Dan Bower of ETH Zurich compared isotope measurements from a wide range of meteorites with Earth's own composition. Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different masses — like siblings who weigh slightly different amounts.

The team used ten isotope systems. Earlier studies usually relied on just two. "Our studies are actually data science experiments," Sossi said. They ran statistical calculations rarely used in geochemistry.

The conclusion: Earth formed entirely from inner Solar System material. Outer material makes up less than 2 percent of Earth's mass — possibly none at all. The study appeared in Nature Astronomy.

"We were truly astonished to find that the Earth is composed entirely of material from the inner Solar System," Bower said.

Scientists divide meteorites into two groups. Non-carbonaceous meteorites formed in the inner Solar System. Carbonaceous ones, richer in water and carbon, came from the outer region. Earth, the analysis says, is made only of the inner kind.

Why two separate reservoirs? Jupiter likely played a role. As the gas giant grew, its gravity carved a gap in the disc of gas and dust around the young Sun. Jupiter acted like a barrier, limiting how much outer material could move inward. Until now, scientists didn't know how effective that barrier was.

The finding suggests Earth grew in a relatively stable environment, gathering nearby planetary bodies. It also means water and other volatiles were probably present in the inner Solar System from the start — no delivery from far away needed.
why_it_matters: This result decides whether the water that fills our oceans was always part of the neighbourhood or arrived by lucky delivery — which changes how likely it is that watery, possibly habitable planets exist around other stars.

background_read: Earth and the other planets grew about 4.6 billion years ago out of a spinning disc of gas and dust left over from the newborn Sun. Close to the Sun it was too hot for water and other light materials to stay solid, so the inner planets — Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars — ended up rocky, while the giant gas planets formed farther out where ices could survive. That dividing line is sometimes called the snow line.

Astronomers fingerprint space rocks by measuring isotopes: slightly different versions of the same chemical element that act like a signature of where a rock formed. Jupiter (the largest planet in our Solar System, a giant ball of gas) grew so massive that its gravity may have split the disc into an inner and an outer zone, keeping the two kinds of material apart.

The new work comes from ETH Zurich (a science and technology university in Switzerland) and was published in Nature Astronomy, a journal for astronomy research. It also fits a trend of 'data science' in geology — instead of one or two measurements, computers compare many at once. If Earth really did form only from nearby material, then the water in our oceans may have been here from the very beginning.

perspectives.description: If Earth was built from nearby material, then water and other volatiles were present close to the Sun from the beginning. That makes watery planets look like a normal outcome of planet formation rather than a lucky accident, which is encouraging for the search for life elsewhere.

Sceptics will note that statistics and ten isotope systems still rest on interpretations of meteorite data, and 'less than 2 percent' is a limit rather than a direct look at Earth's birth. The debate has swung before and may swing again.

perspectives.perspective: A familiar pattern in planetary science
perspectives.description: Planetary science often moves from dramatic explanations toward quieter, local ones as measurement precision improves. The argument echoes earlier fights over the Moon's origin, which were only settled when new samples and better models arrived.

Future asteroid missions and better computer simulations could test the claim directly by sampling material from both reservoirs. If Jupiter's gap really was such an effective barrier, similar gaps may shape planet formation around other stars — something new telescopes might eventually detect.
